Level 2 · Intermediate · Week 10

Project Studio 1

Plan first, then build the core: a small program that works beats a big one that does not.

What you will learn

  • How to turn your project plan into pseudocode and a flowchart.
  • How to split your project into functions, and split the work fairly with your partner.
  • How to build the core loop of your project: the smallest version that runs (Milestone M2).
  • How to review a partner’s code kindly and usefully.

The big idea: build a skateboard first

If you want to build a car, you do not start with one perfect wheel. Nobody can ride a wheel! You build a skateboard first: tiny, but you can ride it. Then a scooter, a bike, a car. Every version works.

Your project works the same way. The core loop is your skateboard:

  • Arcade Game: a window, a player that moves with the keys, and a timer loop that keeps running (screen.ontimer).

  • Art Studio: a while loop that asks what to do (draw, save, load, quit) and does it.

No score, no title screen, no fancy colors yet. Those come later, and they are easy once the skeleton walks.

Pseudocode and flowcharts

Pseudocode is your program written in plain English, one step per line, before you write Python. A flowchart draws the same steps as shapes joined by arrows. Three shapes are all you need: ovals for start and end, rectangles for steps, and diamonds for yes/no questions. Here is the flowchart for a catching game:

The same plan as pseudocode:

set up the screen, the player and the keys
repeat every tick:
move every falling thing down
if a falling thing touches the player: add 1 to the score
if the game is over: save the high score and stop

Every line that does one job can become a function. “Move the player but not off the screen” becomes next_x(x, direction): the position and direction go in, the new position comes out. That is decomposition: breaking a big problem into small named parts.

Exercise10.1: Paper prototype and plan check (M1)

  1. Draw your screen on paper. Use coins for things that move.

  2. One partner is “the computer”, the other is the player. Play for one minute: every clap is one tick.

  3. Finish your plan: write the pseudocode (or draw the flowchart) for your core loop below.

Exercise10.2: A fair task board

Write each function on its own sticky note. Fill in the table, then take turns choosing tasks: one each, like picking teams. Move notes from TO DO to DOING to DONE as you work.

Function name What goes in What comes out Who Done

Exercise10.3: Build the core loop (M2)

Make a folder for your team’s project and save your program as mygame.py (or mystudio.py). Never call it turtle.py! Build it in small steps and press F5 after each one. For an arcade game, the heart of the program is a loop that runs itself again:

the timer loop

def game_loop():
    if not state["running"]:
        return
    # TODO: move falling things, check for catches, add to the score
    screen.update()
    screen.ontimer(game_loop, 50)   # run again in 50 milliseconds

Exercise10.4: Partner code review

Swap seats with your partner (or another team). Run their program and read their code. Then write two stars and a wish: two things that are really good, and one kind idea. Be specific: “the name next_x tells me exactly what it does” helps more than “nice”.

Wish:

Reflect

What was the smallest version of your project that worked today?

Was your task split fair? What would you change next week?

New words

pseudocode
a plan for a program written in plain words, one step per line.
flowchart
a drawing of a program: ovals for start and end, rectangles for steps, diamonds for yes/no questions.
decomposition
breaking a big problem into small parts you can name and build one at a time.
core loop
the part of a game or app that repeats over and over; the smallest version that works.
milestone
a checkpoint on the way to the finished project, like M2 “core loop works”.
code review
reading someone else’s code to help them find bugs and make it clearer.

Homework: Project Studio 1

15–20 minutes. Do Core first; Challenge and Creative are optional.

TipNo computer at home this week?

That is fine. Do the paper parts (the dev log, the Challenge plan and the Creative sketch) and bring them next week. Your project files stay in your team folder; never email or upload them.

CoreFinish your own sticky notes (about 10 minutes)

  1. Open your team’s project in Thonny. Pick one sticky note from your TO DO column that is yours.

  2. Build it in small steps. Press F5 after each step. Save with Cmd+S often.

  3. If you get a red error, read the last line of the traceback and the line number it points to. Stuck for 5 minutes? Write down what you tried and stop: that is useful too.

  4. Write a short dev log (developer diary) below.

What I worked on:

What broke, and how I fixed it (or what I tried):

What I will do next:

ChallengeTests on paper, before the code

Next week you will write pytest tests. Get ahead: choose one of your functions that returns something and write three examples of what goes in and what should come out. Make at least one an edge case (a value at the very limit, like the edge of the screen or a score of 0).

Function and input Expected answer Normal or edge?
next_x(0, 1) 20 normal

CreativeTitle screen sketch

Design the title screen for your project on squared paper: its name, a picture, and one line that explains the keys (“← → to move, space to start”). Use colors from the Okabe–Ito palette (orange, sky blue, bluish green, yellow, blue, vermillion, reddish purple) and make sure nothing depends on color alone. Use your nickname, not your real name.

Self-checkSelf-check: tick each box when it is true
